column3: Near-verbatim parallel: the messenger may destroy himself in grief because they do not believe.
A people reject a messenger despite a sign; it only broadly recalls belief's nonautomatic response.
It explicitly divides people between belief and turning away, supplying the response at issue in the focus.
The statement of nonbelief supports the focus's concern, though it has no messenger or grief dimension.
The immediate continuation distinguishes imposed bodily submission from the inward belief sought in the focus.
Belief is not produced at another person's will but occurs within God's permission.
It directly rejects forcing people to become believers, clarifying the limit behind the focus's grief.
The demand for a sign illustrates the same surah's resistant response to a messenger.
It shows that even decisive signs do not make later belief beneficial, limiting sign-based persuasion.
Chosen passivity and sealed understanding offer only a distant account of persistent nonresponse.
Jesus responds to disbelief by seeking committed supporters, a contrasting messenger response.
It assigns each believer responsibility for himself rather than for another person's straying.
Within the same surah, even clear recitation does not mechanically produce belief.
Moses's constricted chest and speech difficulty resonate with the burden of prophetic rejection.
The verse names the scarcity of belief in the message, though without the focus's emotional limit.
Its inward-self language and fear concern a different personal and legal situation.
Security in a place is not the inward belief or messenger grief addressed by the focus.
Faith's release from fear and sorrow provides only an indirect contrast to the messenger's sorrow.
The messenger is charged only with his own duty while still exhorting believers.
It explicitly commands patience and forbids grieving or remaining constricted over opponents.
The self-reproaching soul shares only the lexical self dimension.
The immediate same-surah refrain joins a manifest sign with the fact that most still do not believe.
Moses fears being killed after rejection, extending the same mission-pressure sequence.
Security from fear uses a different sense of the root and no belief-response relation.
It directly removes responsibility from the messenger for another person's failure to purify himself.
The followers' fear at crisis shows the pressure surrounding the same prophetic mission narrative.
Its question asks what message could induce belief after prior rejection, paralleling persuasion's limit.
Enemies' wish that believers disbelieve is a hostile setting, not the focus's pastoral concern.
A cosmic sign without an explicit belief response is only a remote parallel.
It qualifies apparent belief, showing that inward acceptance cannot be assumed from profession alone.
It describes the marks of believers rather than the messenger's relation to nonbelievers.
God's reassurance to proceed with the mission answers the fear that follows the focus's opening concern.
The verse concerns insecurity before punishment, not belief or prophetic grief.
Their failure to hear and see gives only an indirect account of refusal.
The same-surah rescue command moves the mission narrative beyond the opponents' response.
A sign is intelligible to believers, complementing the focus's concern that others do not believe.
Private remembrance and vigilance concern the messenger's devotion, not another's response.
The merciful greeting has no substantial link to disbelief or prophetic strain.
Signs within selves share only the self vocabulary, not the focus's relation.
The immediate narrative identifies the unjust people to whom the prophetic mission is directed.
The immediately preceding verse establishes the clear Book whose reception is at stake in 26:3.
It simply identifies Noah as a believing servant.
Its command to hold oneself patiently with devoted people provides a related discipline of the self.
Moses anticipates denial, a concrete prophetic anxiety within the nearby mission sequence.
A pressured claim of belief does not directly address the focus's grief over nonbelief.
Fear of people versus God is not the inability to compel belief.
Striving benefits one's own self, limiting the idea that effort can secure another's inward response.
It identifies Abraham as a believing servant without engaging refusal or messenger burden.
A call to piety is only generally related to prophetic exhortation.
The sound heart concerns final acceptance, not the focus's immediate concern for hearers.
Persecution of believers is a distinct situation from grief over unbelief.
The prohibition of transgression in the balance has no material connection.
Rescue and a sign for the worlds only broadly resemble the messenger-and-sign setting.
It identifies two servants as believers without a response or burden parallel.
It commands patience in the face of what opponents say, a practical answer to prophetic strain.
The command to address Pharaoh continues the same-surah commissioning sequence.
Breaking or keeping a pledge returns on the person himself, reinforcing individual moral consequence.
It announces believers' success but does not address those who refuse belief.
The same-surah declaration of death and revival lacks a direct response-to-message link.
Creation as a sign for believers is a distant counterpart to signs not producing belief.
It directly asks why people do not believe, though without the messenger's grief.
Creation and human selves have no specific relation to unbelief or prophetic duty.
It identifies Elijah as a believing servant without engaging rejection.
A messenger facing nonbelief requests separation rather than coercing belief.
The request to release Israel concerns the mission's political demand, not belief.
The common-origin account uses self language in an unrelated creation scene.
Self-accounting makes each person answer for his own record, limiting transferred responsibility.
Commercial fairness has no substantial relation to the focus.
The magicians' belief after a decisive encounter supplies a same-surah instance of genuine response.
Its question about affirmation does not concern a messenger's burden over others.
The greeting scene has no direct belief or grief connection.
Belief frames the benefit of just commerce, only generally related to prophetic calling.
The messenger is told not to comply with deniers, a related limit on engagement with rejection.
The immediate continuation states that every renewed reminder is met by turning away.
Common human origin does not address the personal response of belief.
Warning the nearest kin defines the messenger's duty without guaranteeing their belief.
The accusation of madness is a same-surah form of rejecting the messenger.
Moses states that he controls only himself and his brother, sharply delimiting responsibility for others.
The charge of fabrication is presented as an expression of their nonbelief.
The announced destruction concerns wrongdoing, not a messenger's inability to produce belief.
Provision as a sign for believers only broadly recalls signs and belief.
It directs the messenger to resist disbelievers through the revelation rather than yield to them.
The immediate sequel records their rejection and the coming consequences of what they mocked.
The pairing of souls has only a lexical self connection.
The verse concerns divine knowledge of Jesus's inner self in a different doctrinal setting.
The messenger's warning and glad tidings present the proper proclamation in response to belief and refusal.
Trustworthy obedience describes the messenger of revelation, not hearers' belief.
People see the ruined town yet do not expect resurrection, showing observation without responsive belief.
The immediate opening of Moses's call provides the commissioning background for the following rejection narrative.
No one bears another's burden, and purification benefits oneself, directly limiting vicarious concern.
The repeated call to piety belongs to the same surah but lacks a direct belief-response link.
New believers ask for patience under persecution, contrasting faith's costly but voluntary response.
The category of those brought near has no specific relation to the focus.
Revelation increases believers in faith but does not address the messenger's burden over those who reject.
The messenger serves as witness while the community bears witness, framing proclamation without coercion.
They condition belief on demanded material signs, illustrating why persuasion cannot be reduced to satisfying demands.
Refusal of worship and final gathering are only broadly related to acceptance and rejection.
The rescue of believers states an outcome but not the focus's concern or limit.
Its conditional warning about justice has no material relation to belief.
Pharaoh falsely treats belief as subject to his prior permission, a coercive foil to inward conviction.
God directly acknowledges that the deniers' speech grieves the messenger, while locating their rejection in denial of His signs.
It addresses the messenger's distress at their turning away and denies that he can supply the decisive sign that would gather them.
Only those who truly hear respond; the unresponsive are outside the messenger's power to make believe.
Each person's seeing or blindness returns upon that person, and the messenger is not appointed as their keeper.
Had God willed they would not have associated partners; the messenger is neither their keeper nor their enforcer.
Even overwhelming signs would not make them believe except by God's will, directly limiting evidential compulsion.
God could have guided all people, making universal belief a matter beyond the messenger's control.
The revelation is sent so that no constriction remains in the messenger's chest as he warns.
The messenger's work is distinguished from the hearers' work, preserving separate responsibility for their response.
No messenger may compel people to accept clear evidence when they are averse to it.
It explicitly says that most people will not believe even when the messenger is eager for them to do so.
Guidance and straying are attributed to God, not to the messenger's ability to satisfy demands for signs.
The messenger is responsible only for delivery; reckoning belongs to God.
After clear speech in every people's language, God guides or leaves astray as He wills.
Even the messenger's longing for their guidance cannot overturn God's judgment concerning those left astray.
If they turn away, the messenger's duty remains only clear delivery.
The truth is announced, then belief and disbelief are left as the hearer's response.
The messenger is sent as bearer of good news and warner, not as one who produces belief.
The dead and the deaf who turn away cannot be made to hear by the messenger.
The messenger cannot guide even the one he loves; God knows and guides the rightly disposed.
After warning of earlier deniers, it limits the messenger's task to clear communication.
The messenger cannot make the dead or the turning-away deaf hear, describing the limit of address.
He cannot guide those blind to their error; only receptive submission answers the call.
It expressly tells the messenger not to let his soul perish in regrets over those led astray.
God makes whom He wills hear, while the messenger cannot make those in graves hear.
The messengers' obligation is only clear delivery, even when the people reject them.
It directly instructs the messenger not to be grieved by what the deniers say.
The messenger conveys the Book, but whoever goes astray does so against himself and he is not their manager.
God watches those who take protectors besides Him; the messenger is not their keeper.
When people turn away, the messenger is not sent as their guardian and his duty is only delivery.
The messenger cannot make the deaf hear or guide those plainly lost.
One whom God leaves astray cannot be guided by another after divine sealing.
The messenger is not a compeller over them; he is commanded only to remind those who heed the warning.
If people turn away, the messenger's responsibility remains clear communication.
The way is shown, while gratitude or ingratitude remains the person's response.
The Quran is a reminder for all worlds, framing proclamation rather than coercion.
Willing to take a straight path is attributed to the hearer, not forced by the messenger.
Even that willing operates within God's will, reinforcing the limit of human control over belief.
The messenger is commanded to remind, defining his role as proclamation.
He is explicitly not set over people as a controller.
